reader.title: Expulsion of Black workers from East Atchison, 1880
bases: A mob forced Black laborers off their jobs and drove them and other Black residents out of town across the river (A1, A3), a workplace expulsion that A3 presents as a 'labor conflict'.

Three papers in Texas, South Carolina and Washington Territory agree that a mob drove Black workers from their jobs at Atchison (A1, A2, A3), though all are distant and may rest on a single underlying dispatch; no local report was found.

summary.text: The expulsion of Black workers from East Atchison was an attack in late July or early August 1880 in which a white mob forced Black laborers off their jobs and drove them and other Black residents across the river into Kansas.
The mob ignored the Mayor of Atchison, and the sheriff at St. Joseph refused to intervene.
Southern Democratic papers cited it as proof that Kansas was no refuge for Black people.
According to an item reprinted in the Washington Standard, contractor C. H. Peck had hired several Black men at $1.25 a day to excavate for Wm. Smith's packing-house in East Atchison, Missouri.
A drunken mob armed with revolvers compelled the Black workers to quit, then stopped work at the brick-yard of Seth Co. and drove its seven Black employees over the river.
Black transfer-team drivers were turned back at the bridge, and Black porters and others in town were hunted up and sent into Kansas.
The Brenham Weekly Banner said the mob "ran nearly all the colored people out of town."
The crowd grew to several hundred and was addressed by the mayor and others urging peace, without effect.
Sheriff Spencer of St. Joseph, telegraphed to come, refused, and the mob was said to hold East Atchison in defiance of "the law and the militia."
Atchison residents with interests in the industries were described as indignant and ready to "take a hand" if Buchanan County officials did not act; no report of arrests was found.
The Brenham Weekly Banner in Texas called the expulsion "the sort of social equality and civil rights they get in free and happy Kansas."
The Orangeburg Democrat in South Carolina blamed an armed mob of "white Republicans" and said Northern "Radicals" would have rejoiced had it happened in the South.
The fullest version ran only on 27 August in the Washington Standard of Olympia, under the heading "Antagonisms" as a labor item, calling the proceedings "disgraceful."
No coverage was found in the Black press or in Atchison or St. Joseph papers.
The Southern editorials placed the attack in Atchison, Kansas, while the Standard's item, the only one with local particulars, placed it in East Atchison, Buchanan County, Missouri.

accounts.label: Atchison news item (reprinted)
accounts.gist: A drunken armed mob in East Atchison, Missouri, forced Black laborers off an excavation and a brick-yard and sent Black workers and residents over the river into Kansas, ignoring the mayor and defying the law.

accounts.label: Southern editorial comment
accounts.gist: A white mob at Atchison, Kansas, drove Black hands from their work and, per the Brenham paper, nearly all Black people from town, offered as proof that Kansas and the Republicans were no refuge.

framing.detail: The Brenham Weekly Banner reported the expulsion as a jibe at 'free and happy Kansas', calling it 'the sort of social equality and civil rights' Black people received there.
The Orangeburg Democrat blamed 'white Republicans' and said that had it happened in South Carolina, Northern 'Radicals' would have rejoiced, but in 'Radical Kansas it is all right'.
The Washington Standard's item, headed 'Antagonisms', called the mob drunken and the proceedings 'disgraceful', while using the slur 'darkkeys' for those expelled.

versions.value: East Atchison, Missouri (Buchanan County), with those expelled sent over the river into Kansas

conflicts.note: A3 is the only report with local detail (contractor, brick-yard, bridge, sheriff, county), so its placement in East Atchison, Missouri, is the better-supported version; A1 and A2 are brief editorial comments from distant papers.

versions.value: Nearly all Black people run out of town
Black workers driven from two establishments
Black workers, drivers, porters and other Black people in town sent over into Kansas

conflicts.note: The reports differ in scope; A3's 'other darkkeys in town were hunted up' supports a general expulsion from East Atchison.

record_check.dossier: MO per the only detailed account (East Atchison, Missouri); KS per two brief editorials.
East Atchison (Missouri side of the river opposite Atchison).
expulsion (workplace expulsion in a labor context).
Late July or early August 1880, before 5 August; no exact date.
A white mob, armed and drunk, growing to several hundred.

info: Late July or the first days of August 1880; 'a few days ago' as of 5 August (A1), 'a few days since' as of 13 August (A2); no exact date given.
East Atchison, Missouri, across the river from Atchison, Kansas, per the fullest account (A3); A1 and A2 place it simply at Atchison, Kansas.

Unnamed Black workers: several men hired at $1.25 a day for an excavation, seven men at a brick-yard, transfer-team drivers, freight-depot porters, and other Black people in town (A3); 'nearly all the colored people' of the town per A1.
None; no crime was alleged against the workers. A3 places the attack in the context of 'labor conflict' after a contractor hired Black men at $1.25 a day.
A mob, described as 'a white mob' (A1), 'an armed mob of white Republicans' (A2), and 'a drunken mob, armed with revolvers' (A3); no individuals named.

sources.note: Short editorial paragraph: a white mob at Atchison 'a few days ago' drove Black hands from brickyards, transfer trains and freight depots and then ran nearly all Black people out of town; mocks Kansas as a refuge.
quotes: At Atchison a few days ago a white mob drove the colored hands from the brickyards, transfer trains, freight depots, etc. After this they ran nearly all the colored people out of town.
This is the sort of social equality and civil rights they get in free and happy Kansas.
